ican.text: I can expand a logarithm of a product, quotient or power using the correct law.
I can combine logarithmic terms into one logarithm when their bases match and arguments are positive.
I can state the domain of an expression containing logarithms before solving an equation.
I can solve and check a logarithmic equation, rejecting values outside the original domain.
I can distinguish a logarithmic law from an invalid operation on a sum or difference.

ku.text: For $a>0$, $a\ne1$ and $x,y>0$, the product law is $\log_a(xy)=\log_a x+\log_a y$.
For the same restrictions, the quotient law is $\log_a(x/y)=\log_a x-\log_a y$.
For $x>0$, the power law is $\log_a(x^m)=m\log_a x$. Apply the laws only where the original expressions are defined; in particular, $\log(x^2)=2\log|x|$ for $x\ne0$.
The syllabus guidance uses bases 10 and $e$ in exam questions. Here $\log x$ means $\log_{10}x$, and $\ln x$ means $\log_e x$.
When solving an equation, first require every argument in the original expression to be positive. Combining logarithms can yield algebraic candidates that fail this original domain.
A logarithm of a sum is not a sum of logarithms: there is no general law $\log(x+y)=\log x+\log y$.

needs: Exponents and the definition of logarithms

misc.better: The product law concerns $\log(xy)$, not $\log(x+y)$. For example, $\log(1+9)=1$, while $\log1+\log9\ne1$.
For $x\ne0$, $\ln(x^2)=2\ln|x|$. The expression $2\ln x$ is defined only for $x>0$.
The order is preserved: $\log x-\log y=\log(x/y)$ for $x,y>0$.

misc.weak: After solving $\log x+\log(x-3)=1$, both algebraic roots are valid.
misc.better: The original arguments require $x>3$, so the negative algebraic root must be rejected.
$\log(2x)=\log2+\log x$ for $x>0$. The expression $2\log x$ equals $\log(x^2)$ when $x>0$.

terms.text: Apply product, quotient and power laws to rewrite a logarithm as a sum or difference, respecting the domain.
Combine terms with the same base using the laws, and ensure each original argument is positive.
State the original domain, solve the transformed equation and check all candidates in the original expression.

formula.text: For $a>0$, $a\ne1$ and $x,y>0$, the booklet gives $\log_a(xy)=\log_a x+\log_a y$, $\log_a(x/y)=\log_a x-\log_a y$ and $\log_a(x^m)=m\log_a x$.

gdc.text: For a base-10 logarithm, use [LOG] followed by the argument, then [EXE]. For a natural logarithm, use [LN] followed by the argument, then [EXE].
Use the solver or a graph to check an equation numerically, but enforce the original logarithm domain before accepting a result.

worked.prompt: Assume $x>0$ where needed and use $\log$ for base 10.

parts.label: (a)
parts.q: Write $\ln12-\ln3$ as a single logarithm and evaluate it to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.a: The original arguments require $x>3$. Combine to get $\log[x(x-3)]=1$, so $x(x-3)=10$. Thus $(x-5)(x+2)=0$. Only $x=5$ satisfies $x>3$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.q: Explain why $x=-2$ cannot be accepted in part (c).
parts.a: At $x=-2$, both $x$ and $x-3$ are negative, so the logarithms in the original equation are not real.

kq.q: Why does multiplying arguments add their logarithms?
kq.model: If $x=a^u$ and $y=a^v$, then $xy=a^{u+v}$. Taking base-$a$ logarithms gives $\log_a(xy)=u+v=\log_a x+\log_a y$.

kq.q: Why can combining logarithms introduce an invalid algebraic root?
kq.model: The combined product may be positive when both original factors are negative. The original separate logarithms still require each argument to be positive.
Because $x^2=|x|^2$ and $|x|>0$, so the power law applies to the positive quantity $|x|$.

kq.q: Why does the order matter when subtracting logarithms?
kq.model: Subtraction corresponds to division in the same order: the first argument is the numerator and the second is the denominator.
